Protoplasm  [Or.  TT^WTOJ,  first,  +  7rAa<r/ia, 
anything  formed  or  moulded]  :  Ger.  /'roto- 
phtsma;  Fr.  protoplasme ;  Ital.  protoptasma. 
The  living  substance  of  the  cell,  exclusive  of 
the  nucleus.  See  LIVING  MATTER. 

The  term  was  introduced  by  v.  Mohl,  and 
rapidly  gained  currency.  The  conception  was 
widely  spread  by  Huxley's  celebrated  lecture, 
The  J'hi/sical  Basis  of  Life,  which,  embodied  the 
results  of  Max  Schult/.e  and  Kiihne.  Proto 
plasm  consists  of  two  materials,  probably  both 
fluids — the  reticulum,  and  the  cell  sap  or 
hyaloplasma  which  fills  the  meshes  of  the 
reticulum.  Two  theories  as  to  the  actual 
structure  are  current:  (i)  according  to 
Flemming,  the  reticulum  consists  of  threads  ; 
(2)  according  to  Biitschli,  the  reticulum  corre-

Ger.  Protozoan,  einzelliges  Tier;  Fr.  proto- 
zoaire  ;  Ital.  protozoa.  An  animal  constituted 
by  a  single  cell,  or  a  group  of  similar  cells. 
The  cells  may  he  multinucleated,  and  the 
body  of  the  cell  may  be  very  considerably 
differentiated.  Cf.  AMOEBA,  AGAMOGENESIS, 
and  CONJUGATION.
